I wish to refer for a moment or two to some statements made yesterday by the hon. member from King's (P.E.I.) (Mr. Hughes) in regard to our national debt. The Finance Minister in his budget speech does not give us very much encouragement as to what is going to happen in the near future in connection with paying any part of our national debt. He says we must soon begin to consider the question of reduction of our public debt, rather than the increase of it. According to the last report that I have been able to obtain from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the national wealth of the Dominion of Canada is estimated at $19,002,778,000. The national debt of the country is about two billion and a half. That is the federal debt; if we take into consideration the provincial, the municipal and the private debts in the Dominion of Canada in addition, I think I am safe in saying that the total debt of the Dominioin of Canada will reach four and a half or five billion dollars, or, in other words, the total debt of the Dominion of Canada will reach about one quarter of our national wealth. I ask hon. members of this House if they consider that is a good position financially for the Dominion of Canada to be in, or, without even looking to the near future, if the time has not already arrived when we should provide some means to retire, at least a portion of our national debt. There re those of us who have been identified with municipal work for many years, and we have found it impossible for a municipality to increase its debenture debt over and above a certain amount, unless by consent of some higher authority than its own. If a municipality increases its debenture debt past a certain amount, restrictions are put upon it by the province or some other authority, which restrictions will immediately bring it to time. If it is right that a municipality should have to make provision for retiring its debenture debt, either by a sinking fund or by making provision in those debentures that, at the end of a certain number of years, the debentures should be retired with an added amount of interest and principal, is it not equally true that in the Dominion some means should be taken, before the time
comes when we are upon the verge of financial disaster, to provide for the payment of at least a part of our national debt?
I wish to approve the words that were spoken by the hon. member for King's, P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes) and to go considerably further. I wish to ask hon. members if they consider that we are carrying out the provisions of the heritage that has been given to us by our pioneer fathers, when we are drifting continually year after year into eighty or ninety million dollars more of debt. I am well aware that, according to the manner in which the finances of the Dominion of Canada are-I was going to say, juggled, if, Sir, you will permit the word without calling me to order-an apparent surplus is shown in some way of $73,000,000, in one year, and in other years of a somewhat larger amount. I feel that I cannot for one moment take that into consideration when the ultimate end of the year's work is an addition to our nation's debt of eighty or ninety million dollars. That is the only standpoint from which it is proper to judge, if it is right to judge at all.
The main reason which prompted me to rise to my feet is that I might protest against the excise duty that has been placed upon the beet sugar factories. It has been inferred by the Minister of Finance that that excise tax of 49 cents per 100 pounds will be met by the sugar factories. I do not at the present time recollect a single instance in which a tax has been placed against any industrial incorporation where that industrial corporation has not by some means transferred that tax to the producer or the consumer. We are told that this tax of one per cent that is imposed upon bank circulation will be met entirely by the banks. I mistake very much the influence or the intelligence of those who comprise the bankers' association, if they do not find some means of transferring this tax to the people with whom they are doing business. If it be possible for the Minister of Finance or for this Government to prevent that from being done, I should certainly be very glad. But as regards this tax of 49 cents per 100 pounds that has been placed upon the sugar refineries, there is no question that that tax will revert to the beet grower. I am not a sugar beet grower myself, so that I have no individual interest to speak about; but m the southern part of the riding which I represent, there is a considerable number of sugar beet growers. I should like to

The Budget-Mr. Fortier
ask why an excise tax is imposed in such a manner that it places a burden upon sugar beet growers, and not upon any other agricultural production. Is this only a start towards imposing an ex-
5 p.m. cise tax upon the whole of agricultural production; or are the sugar beet growers especially marked out for this particular tax? I think if the Minister of Finance would consider that the application of this excise tax is a direct blow at the sugar beet growers, he would reconsider this tax; or if it is going to be continued, then I think we have every reason to ask that every other line of agricultural industry and every other line of industry in general shall also be subjected to an excise tax. I believe this country would be better off to-day with an excise tax than with a protective tariff. I go further than that; I believe that if upon every commodity that could be taxed, a reasonable excise tax were placed, it would be a very few years before the whole of our national debt would be paid. Allow me to say, in conclusion, that I do not consider that any great bouquets are handed out to the farmers by the 2i per cent reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. Mention has been made that this 21 per cent reduction is going to reduce our revenue. I cannot see that. A reduction in any tariff that affects the protected industries in this country does not reduce the revenue, for the simple reason that that revenue does not go into the coffers of the Dominion. I am not making any special plea for the beet growers; I am not making any special plea for the farmers; I stand before you to-day and I say on my behalf and, I hope, on behalf of the whole of the farmers amongst whom I am sitting, that we are not asking for any special privileges, but that we are asking for the right to stand upon the one broad platform of equality with every industry in the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my first words on
this all important question of the budget will be that of congratulations to the distinguished statesman, who for the sixteenth time has delivered, in this House, the Liberal Government's budget. The whole country applauds the Prime Minister's achievement in having gathered within his cabinet, such eminent colleagues from all the provinces of the Dominion. No epoch can be compared to this present one, if we may except that memorable time of 1896,

when Laurier surrounded himself with so many illustrious statesmen. At that time, the province of Nova Scotia was possessed of one of these eminent men, in the person of its Prime Minister. After fifteen years of judicious and faithful services to his country as Minister of Finance, this distinguished statesman, highly respected by all members in this House, once more returns, notwithstanding his advanced age, to take up his share of work and his post of honour. At a time when the country is greatly in need of its very best brains, he comes forth to place his intellectual powers, his experience and his patriotism - at the disposal of his beloved Canada. In reviewing our present political history, I cannot find a more noble example than that which ;is given to the present and rising generation, by this veteran in political life, by this unrivalled parliamentarian, by this distinguished statesman, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).
Mr. Speaker, I approve the Government's policy. In this budget speech, I see the fulfilment, as near as circumstances will permit, of the liberal party's programme; this policy is for the welfare of the country and its beneficient effects are already being felt. I shall just add a word touching the amendment moved by the official opposition. The country is but little interested in the object aimed at by the Conservative party. This attempt to embarrass the Government by taunts for not accomplishing that in which one has no faith or takes objection to, is but to seek party advantage against the country's own interests. In my opinion, it is poor strategy and the Progressive party soon discovered the weak point. Is the Conservative opposition sincere when they reproach the Government for not having sufficiently cut down the tariff?
If so, what has become of their platform, their Vaunted national policy, so called? What has become of their recent political declaration which the country has just heard and which was spurned by the people at the last general elections?
We must acknowledge facts and meet the necessity of the moment. The revenue demands the maintenance of adequate taxation; the lowering of the tariff must be accomplished by degrees and the first step taken as shown by the budget is in the right direction. The increase in taxes is justified by the duty we are under of clearing our national debt. These taxes have

The Budget-Mr. Fortier
become necessary to meet our obligations. War has gobbled everything. Our fate, for generations to come, is to pay war pensions and to shelter under our guardianship the returned soldiers.
WTe, of the Liberal party and especially those who were opposed to certain measures which have dragged the country into expenditures far too great for a young nation, did not wish to overstep the just limits which our obligations called for; however, the majority demanded it, the debt has been incurred, it would be dishonourable to repudiate it: and if we are not permitted to disavow the obligations that Canada has contracted, it is absolutely necessary that the taxes be increased.
There is, Mr. Speaker, one tax in particular that I wish to refer briefly to. It is the income tax. If there is an assessment which may be looked upon as loathsome, it is certainly this one. It is a heavy burden carried by the ratepayer, and what is most depressing is that we cannot entertain any hope of relief in the near future. We have perhaps, within these last years, lost the opportunity of throwing the whole burden on the profiteers who amassed wealth during the war. However, we should endeavour to relieve the workman and the small trader and to make up for such losses by imposing a higher tax on luxuries. It seems to me that the people we should spare, should be the heads of families. I therefore beg of the Government to reduce the tax which the heads of families have to pay. In my opinion, a father having five children should not be called upon to pay income tax until his revenue reaches $5,000, and if he happens to be the father of eight children he should not pay income tax until his revenue reaches $10,000.
Our vast country, abounding in natural resources of all kinds, has not the necessary population for the so much desired development of our commercial, farming and mining industries. What we are in need of, is a greater increase in population. Not being able to obtain the desired increase from oui countrymen, we are forced to seek it in immigration. What can we expect from immigration? The European countries have been desolated by war. France, whose population has been decimated by this awful war is encouraging repopulation by granting a bonus to parents of numerous children. Parents under 30 years of age, having five children, receive from the state a grant of 10,000 francs, and those who have eight children receive 25,000 francs. It is true, we are not in a position to make such gifts owing to our present financial state of affairs. Nevertheless one of the statesmen of my province, who played an important part in the progress of old Quebec, and whose memory the people still cherish-Mercier- had legislation passed, granting 100 acres of land to the father of twelve living children. It is by giving a better interpretation to the benevolent laws of that province and of this country which is dear to us, that we should, it seems to me, consider the possibility of reducing as much as we can the income tax, taking also into consideration the obligations which devolve on the heads of families. The present expenditures are not all an outcome of the war, for the budget has also to reckon with the yearly deficit of the railways acquired by the state. It is a sad legacy inherited by the Government which the people chose in December last. Let us hope that these statesmen will not fail in their duty and that under their able administration, the present sad plight of our railways will be followed by a new era of prosperity. To my judgment, one may discuss the question of nationalization of railways indefinitely and never come to a lasting solution. I shall therefore not undertake to discuss this subject. France itself has administered five industries with more or less success. To-day its economists are still discussing without any satisfactory solution, the expediency of the management of railways by the state. For my part, without leaning one way or the other in the controversy in which those pro and con are thus engaged, I cannot help thinking that the greatest objection to state ownership is that, while a private company has always the profits in view, the state very unfortunately has at its disposal a tax to cover the deficits; however, I rather think that in a new country like ours, colonization is of primary national importance and for the success of which, we must uphold our railway policy. A private company has no interest in investing its capital in uninhabited regions or of investing such capital without being certain of an immediate return. We must not depend on private companies to further our policy of settling this country. History teaches us that privately owned companies have never answered to the needs of colonization. It was the provincial governments that built the railways


The Budget-Mr. Fortier
across the desert prairies or through the virgin forests when the Dominion government failed to do so or did not furnish all the means of accomplishing such a task by its grants in money or land. When the railway had paved the way into those regions and had become a paying proposition, it was eagerly sought by some large private concern that very readily annexed it to its system as a source of profit. I am pleased to see that, owing perhaps to unforeseen circumstances, most of our railways are now managed by the state. Perhaps the time has come for us to press our just demands, so as to forward the settlement of our newly opened districts, as I intend to do for the county of Labelle which I have the honour to represent in this House. Private companies have already built lines up to the borders of the county, but on account of financial difficulties-which are the cause of failure in operating a railway in these new settlements

the work of construction was discontinued. I am pleased to see that the Canadian National Railway is now the property of the state. This railway extends from the metropolis of Canada into the Laurentians, reaches the borders of the county of Labelle, at a place called Huberdean, and I still hope, for the sake of the people of the county, that this railway will penetrate to its very centre. Natural resources abound in that part of Canada. The settlers, not without great sacrifices, have cleared the land and have established parishes which are at a great distance from the railway. This may have perhaps shocked some of the heralds of imperialism and militarism, but it has brought joy to the great majority in this country and I may add that it has specially pleased the people in the county of Labelle. However, where this decrease is most in evidence, to the satisfaction of
[Mr. Fortier. 1
everybody, it is in the militia expenditures. I hail with pleasure this new policy which will second the efforts of the country in reducing to its right proportion its standing army.
Let us return to peace pursuits. Let us economize and pay our debts. Such must be the motto of the Liberal party which the people have called upon to administer the affairs of the country, such must be the all designated goal towards which all our statesmen should tend, so as to save us from ruin and lead us on to great and nobler destinies.

Mr. Speaker, some sixteen years ago I happened to be a student of the University of Toronto, and I remember picking up the evening paper of the 30th November, 1906, and reading the budget speech of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). All will remember in those days the dominant figures of the Liberal party were their distinguished leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the then and present Minister of Finance. It is interesting to observe in this newspaper, which I hold in my hand, that in that budget speech certain changes not of a substantial nature, but, on the contrary, of comparatively minor importance, were made. In place of the general S&V3 discount on British goods, there was substituted a special discount on each article, with some increases. Duties were slightly reduced, chiefly on agricultural implements, such as reapers, mowers and binders, and also on confectionery, gasoline, oranges, and lemons; duties were increased on hats, canned meats, beans, peas, and other vegetables-and it is wonderful to behold in those days the duties were also increased on horses and cattle.
Before proceeding further, I desire to tender my sincere wishes for the long-continued health and happiness of the Minister of Finance. We younger members look with respect and admiration on his distinguished career. Sixteen years ago his ideas were advantageous to me as a young man studying our fiscal policy, and they are equally advantageous to me to->day when he has become in fact the anchor of his party. Of course, now and again we see the ship of state blown hither and thither by the gentle winds from the West which, zephyr-like, blow upon the nervous brows of many hon. members of the Government. We may find some day that those zephyrs will develop hurricane force, which will again divide this country on those great

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
economic principles of free trade and protection. If I were a prophet, I would suggest that the political thought of Canada to-day is moving in that direction and that the present partnership of the Liberal and Progressive parties is not destined to be permanent, that sooner or later the economic questions which differentiate them will rise up and overthrow all those unimportant considerations which now hold them together. In this newspaper of 1906 it is interesting to note the headlines in respect to the estimates. For instance, we find the following:
Estimates are $105,000,000. Reach stupendous figure.
It is an interesting observation in psychology to see what really is in men's minds in considering the relative importance of the great questions confronting the country. Our friends on the prairies are making a great fuss for the reduction of duties on agricultural implements, but when you come to examine the effect of that reduction upon business and upon the operations of our commercial enterprises, you find that it really comes to practically nothing. In 1906 it was considered that $105,000,000 was a stupendous figure for the estimates; what would the same people think of to-day's estimate, which is really stupendous, reaching a figure of $425,000,000 or more? It shows that the people are capable of doing more than they sometimes believe they can do.
Does the hon. member mean 1896 or 1906?
I mean 1906. It is the Mail and Empire, I must confess, but the date of publication would hardly be wrong, though many other things in it might be.
If it is the hon. minister's (Mr. Fielding's) first budget speech, it would be in 1896.

No, it is not the minister's first budget speech; it is the speech of 1906. As I hold the paper up the hon. member may see the headlines of the article from where he sits. But the point I am anxious to make in that connection is that the proposals brought forward in these various budget speeches are very different from the promises made in the preceding elections. In 1893 it was free trade just as they had it in England. In 1896 more mature judgment prevailed-I do not doubt but that the soundness of the judgment of the pre'sent Minister of Finance was the cause-and the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald and the Conservative party was adhered to, as was obviously necessary in the best interests of the country. Then we come again to 1906, and notwithstanding all the preachings with respect to free trade, the straight and narrow path in the best interests of the country was followed; the national policy was continued, with some slight deviations, to which I referred a moment ago. Then, coming to 1919, we find another splurge for free trade-a promise of reduction on nineteen specific articles and a substantial reduction on all others. But in 1922, with the present Minister of Finance at the helm, the good old Conservative policy is adhered to, because the minister knows, and responsible men charged with the administration of the affairs of the country know, that they cannot safely depart from that policy. I venture a prediction that my hon. friends of the Progressive party would not, if they were called upon to form a government, deviate from the policy which the Minister of Finance announced to the House a few days ago. The change from opportunity to criticise freely to responsibility for government brings about also a change of attitude at the last moment with respect to these matters. Now, these doctrines have been enunciated not only in political platforms, but in campaign speeches and literature up to the very moment of the election. I have before me the speech of the hon. Prime Minister delivered in Vancouver, in which he lays down the same Liberal platform, viz, substantial downward revision of the tariff which had been long overdue.
I propose to give to the House a few words uttered by the Minister of Finance at the great Liberal convention in August, 1919. These are golden words, and I hope the Minister of Finance is listening with one ear as I repeat them. I quote from the Globe of August 8, 1919:
Sincerity is a great thing in politics. It should be. Politics is not a mere game and should not be a game; and it is a poor, miserable game when they do things merely to win power.
Now, I say that these are golden words, and they should be inscribed over every entrance to this chamber. I am not suggesting for a moment that the minister himself has deviated from the principle enunciated in these words, but I fear there are forces about him which have swayed

the ship of state from [DOT]the course which might otherwise have been followed. I say, Sir, that these words should be treasured in our memory and written in our hearts. But it is not only the Minister of Finance who discusses this doctrine of sincerity and who utters these philosophic words. There were other persons at this convention, some of whom are now members of the Government, while some have been passed on to the Senate. Senator Pardee said to the convention:
If we are to succeed; if Canada is to succeed, it will not be enough to enunciate policies. They must be brought into operation. They must be rightly administered with earnestness, sincerity, efficiency and honesty.

We have also an editorial from the Toronto Globe. Before passing to that, let me say that these ideals were put forward with a view to convincing the people that the policies formulated would be carried out. They were preached from pulpit and platform; they were embodied in philosophic utterances; they were stated with apparent sincerity and earnestness. It is, therefore, the course of consistency on the part of hon. members on this side to move the amendment which they have proposed in connection with the budget. Liberalism has made a covenant with the people of Canada. The delegates to the national convention have pledged the Liberal party to certain specific reforms should the electorate entrust the government of the Dominion to the Parliamentary representatives of the party under its new leader, the Hon. Mackenzie King, who will doubtless be provided at once with a seat so that he may again take a place in the House after an absence of almost eight years from the political arena.
The article continues:
The pledges concerning tariff reform and the efforts to be made to reduce the cost of living are much more specific than political conven-
\Mr. Ladner.]
ventions usually make. The country will expect that the promises now made shall be implemented if after the next general election a Liberal ministry is formed. There was no truer word spoken at the convention than the statement of Premier Norris of Manitoba that the time has arrived in the history of Canada when the people will make the politicians keep their promises.
Here in this chamber are the people's representatives from the Prairie provinces possessed of those high ideals; and to-day we on this side of the House have moved an amendment. Here is the opportunity of my hon. friends to my left to make these politicians keep their promises. I have stressed that feature considerably because it is pertinent and relevant to the amendment which we are moving, and because I believe that as a young member of this Parliament, I should proclaim my own opposition to a species of election campaign extending from one end of the country to the other in which promises were given that are not fulfilled, and in regard to which no explanations are forthcoming. There is not a great deal of change in the tariff under the present budget. There is a reduction of from 21 to 5 per cent, but little tendency shown to carry out the policies enunciated at the Liberal convention of 1919. There is no substantial reduction at all, and I am glad that no important changes have been made. For the benefit of my friends to my left and some of our eastern friends sitting opposite, I should like to give the situation in the city of Vancouver. There is a city which has developed very rapidly in the past few years, and its outlook is one of industrial and maritime expansion. We have in the city of Greater Vancouver, 687 factories, employing nearly 19,000 employees, and there are some 60,000 souls dependent on these industries. If the protective tariff were taken away, it would be a death blow to - the development of that city and to British Columbia, because their outlook must be on-e of industrial and commercial development. Nearby we have the great

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
nation of Japan. With its cheap labour and low standards of living, Japan can send its goods to Canada manufactured at one-fifth the labour cost prevailing in this country, and how is it possible for,the industries and the workmen of this country to compete with those goods, or with the goods that are made by cheap German labour? It cannot be done. I say again that once our friends on my left became charged with the responsibilities of office, they themselves would not advocate many of the ideas which they advocate to-day. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) said that our national policy was based on a fallacy and experience had proven this to be so. I would like to put to him and to others what the real objects of protection are. In my opinion, they are to diminish as far as possible the importation from foreign countries of goods which can be produced at approximately the same cost at home; to facilitate the importation of raw material which cannot be produced at home; to encourage the manufacture of Canadian materials into the finished product, and their exportation; to make Canada self-contained by encouraging and developing within her borders all the legitimate activities that will give occupation to her people; and lastly, to secure revenue.
What have been the results of this policy? When you compare what this country was in 1878, or even at Confederation, with conditions now, you will see the great development that has taken place in this country under the protective policy, under a policy of reasonable protection such as sixty-three of the civilized countries of the world have retained since the war-and many of them have increased their tariff. In the light of their experience we can hardly pursue a different policy. In the year 1867 we had a population of 3,000,000 people; to-day we have a population of 9,000,000. Then we had a railway mileage of 2,280; to-day we have a mileage of about 39,000. In 1867 we had 123 branch banks; to-day we have 4,500. We have now 800,000 farms comprising over 53,000,000 acres of land, according to recent statistics. We had in 1867 3,800,000 head of live stock; in 1921 we had 15,500,000 head. There was invested in manufacturing business in this country in 1867, $78,000,000; to-day there is invested over $3,000,000,000. The public revenue at Confederation was $90,000,000; to-day it is in the neighbourhood of $425,000,000 or $450,000,000. Our exports at the time of Confederation were $52,000,000 worth of goods; our exports
to-day amount to about $1,250,000,000. These are the results of the policy of reasonable protection which as been followed in this country. It is all right to stand up in this Chamber and say: Oh, it is a bad policy; you should not follow a policy of that kind; if we had free trade, we would get cheaper agricultural machinery, and this, that, and the other thing cheaper; but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the test of a policy is its results, and the results of protection in this country cannot be denied. They may be argued, tout they cannot be denied. The other course has not been followed in this country, but we have the experience of a number of other nations to determine whether or not it would have 'been a wise policy for this country to follow.
In concluding my remarks I would like to point out what I consider to be the two chief weaknesses of this budget. The first is that provision which enables German goods to come to Canada in large quantities with practically no restriction. In my opinion that is an unsound policy. It is unsound because of the cheapness of labour over there, and 'because of their lower standards of living forced upon them by their own iniquities in their outrage on civilization. To-day they are in the position of having committed these iniquities against'civilization, and now we are putting them in a position to ship their goods here. I submit that that principle is unsound. I say that you cannot by logic eliminate sentiment in this country. I maintain that men who will look with real perspective across the Atlantic will not raise their eyes from the thousands of crosses in Flanders fields across over to the Rhine where the Hun holds out his bloody hand. I ibelieve the people of this country do not want us to grasp his hand just because we could make a good deal with him. The people of this country do not want to save the last cent by the complete abnegation of all sentiment and sympathy and regard for the 56,000 men who lie over there, and who gave their lives for other things than trade. It is repugnant to the finer sense of the people of this country, and the Government will find that out before they have followed this policy very long. What will the men in the military hospitals, who are incapacitated for life, think of it? Picture them picking up their newspapers and reading that the Government of Canada have, a little over three years after the war, broken down the barriers against German goods, and that their baskets and toys and their

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
things of that kind that they are making will have to compete with German toys and other goods sent over here. You may say it is all sentiment. Of course it is sentiment. But it was sentiment that brought about a successful issue of the war, and it is sentiment that will keep Canada united and will preserve our Empire. The Government should think carefully before it enters upon this course and should not allow itself to be swayed by the words of the Minister of Finance when he says it is humbugging the world to pretend that we are protecting ourselves against Germany. Those are high sounding words but they do not constitute an argument sufficient to override the policy which was adopted in the past of keeping German goods out; and if you ask the people of this country whether they would admit those goods or keep them out ninety-nine out of every hundred will express themselves in favour of a policy of exclusion.
Another objection I have to the budget is in connection with the sales tax. We have here the introduction of a principle of direct taxation which appeals strongly to our Progressive friends. The indirect taxation which was found in the former protective tariff has been eliminated, but the substitution of direct for indirect taxation will*not only prove unpopular with the mass of working people of this country but will be a positive injury to them. It would have been far better to have secured revenue by the old-time method, than to raise it by a form of taxation which imposes a burden upon many of the people who are less able than others to pay it.

This undoubtedly works against the best interests of the Canadian fruit industry; and practical common sense would convince one of the necessity of having an anti-dumping regulation for the protection of our own fruit growers. tects the fruit growers there to the fullest extent, but there is no hindrance to their dumping in Canada, and our fruit industry accordingly suffers. To allow the United States growers to pursue such a policy is both unsound and unwise.
To-day I received a letter from a little storekeeper in the suburbs of Vancouver. The writer is a returned man, and he deals in his letter with the sales tax. I shall quote briefly from the communication because the writer expresses the idea in a . far better way than I could myself. He says:
I did not complain at the luxury tax during war time, hut I do now strongly protest at a 5 per cent tax on what is the children's delight, the poor man's meal-a five cent hox of chocolate. Why tax candy and leave jewellery free?
I do not know whether jewellery is left free, but if such is the case I think this man's objection is well founded. There is no reason why confectionery, which is used to a greater extent by the majority of people than articles of luxury, should be taxed while jewellery is left untouched.
I conclude my remarks by reminding our friends on the Government side that we must judge the future by the events of the past. The history of Canada is before us. It rises like an immense column on which we may see inscribed the soundest maxims of political experience. We must take wisdom from the examples of others; we must derive encouragement from their success and learn caution from their misfortunes. We must look back upon the history of the nations that have gone before, we can look back upon the history of our own country, and from the lessons we learn we may be guided for the future in such a way as to avoid pitfalls and make the people of this country a happy, prosperous and contented nation.

If the people throughout the country are in a more or less feverish state of mind and if, during the last year, we have had labour troubles and numbers of unemployed men, many of whom no doubt have known what it was to suffer the pangs of want, we have also a large mercantile class who are feeling the pinch of poverty just the same as the farming and labouring classes, by reason of the fact that their business is depressed, and I think they were justified in expecting some relief when we had this new Government elected. I am a little afraid that that relief is not forthcoming in this 2i per cent reduction in the tariff and the 50 per cent increase in the sales tax. The budget can, to my mind, give them little encouragement.
I should like briefly to allude to the final appeal of the Minister of Finance, who in his concluding words called upon labour and capital to get together. I could not help thinking that probably there was, on the part of the Government, a desire which they found it impossible for them to implement and that probably the unseen hand which controls governments and the destinies of nations was at work when the budget was being drafted. Our need today is a government that is big enough, strong enough, and fearless enough to try to lessen the gulf that exists between our social classes. We have on the one hand a display of social exclusiveness and on the other a display of want and suffering. Our people are fast being divided into two classes, one paying interest and the other collecting it. Having in mind these things, the condition that our people are in and what they might naturally expect, I cannot recommend this budget, as brought down by the Government, as being worthy of their best attempts.
The other evening the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), when speaking in the House, laid stress on the fact that 
in 1892 this country was in a similar or worse condition in comparison with that of to-day. I believe he sought to argue that because we had got out of that depression all right, there was no reason to think we should not get out of this one. The hon. gentleman is on very dangerous ground. Surely it is not well to argue that because we have got into deep water and come out all safe, we are safe in bobbing up and down in deep water perpetually and at will. Conditions at that time were altogether different from what they are to-day At that time we had little or no national debt. Now we have a federal debt of about $2,500,000,000, and added to that we have our various provincial and municipal d;bts. Therefore, every citizen in Canada can feel that on him devolves the necessity of paying interest on three separate debts, outside of what he may owe himself, and unfortunately many of us owe money. I maintain that the interest on these debts and the cost of civil government-and by the way that is another cost which is rapidly mounting up; I think probably at the present time our bootlegging industry is costing the country as much as our entire civil government did twenty years ago-must all be charged up against our production and against what we can develop from our natural resources. I believe the time is very near at hand when we shall find that it will take our entire production to pay the interest on our debts, and when that time comes we shall be facing absolute bankruptcy as a nation.
This Government, if it hopes to avoid such a catastrophe, will have to evolve something that is more fitting to relieve our depression than the present budget. I might say further that I am thoroughly convinced that before we can hope to re-establish our national standing and to get our country back to a prosperous condition, we shall have to change our credit system. I am thoroughly convinced that it is absolutely unworkable for any length of time, and unless we change our credit system, I cannot see where we have any possibility of lessening this huge debt.

The hon. gentleman from Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) is entirely welcome to say that it was a pronouncement sealing the doom of high protection. " Sir, do you know that I can prove to you there is no such place as Heaven?" The old clergyman took no notice and continued reading his newspaper. Again he

Perhaps it is an example of the lingering death of party spirit that the budget itself has not been received with the same unanimous acclaim and enthusiasm, but we on this side of the House are in hopes that with the presentation of a few more consecutive "budgets by our distinguished Minister of Finance we may have that happy consummation.
Down in Nova Scotia the people perceived, long before the declaration of the polls, that the late administration was doomed to defeat, and I may tell the House that we formed a little plan to celebrate this occasion. We knew that the hopes of the people were centred on the man who in years gone by had turned the chronic Foster deficits into the chronic Fielding surpluses, and recognizing him as the one and only outstanding choice for the position of Minister of Finance in the new Liberal administration, the .people of Nova Scotia decided to celebrate his sixteenth budget by sending here one Liberal representative, including his distinguished self, for every budget that he had presented to this House and to the country. We carried out that scheme, and our only regret is that we could not do more, because our efforts entailed no self-sacrifice; on the morning of the 7th December the men who had tried to stand in the road of that tremendously popular movement woke up to find that

they had lost their deposits. And, Sir, [DOT]we congratulate the country that for the sixteenth time the man whose budgets were such a pronounced success for fifteen consecutive times is to-day the man who has been chosen to bring down this budget to Parliament and the country at a time of the most critical financial stress that we have ever experienced.
There is no doubt in the world that some hon. members are disappointed that the tariff reductions are not greater. One thing we on the Liberal side promised the country, and I think our Progressive friends also made the same promise, that whatever our ultimate views as to the tariff, whether it should be high or low, in this time of recovery from the staggering blow of the war, from the amazing deficits that the railway policy of the late government had imposed upon our young country, this was not the time to attempt any drastic tariff changes that would dislocate the business of the country. Therefore when some of us are disappointed that the tariff reductions are not greater, I would ask them to remember that promise.
Our hon. friends opposite would have us believe that the country was looking for the full and literal translation of the Liberal tariff platform of 1919. Well, I was struck with the remark which fell from the right hon. leader of the Opposition the other day, when he pointed out that freight rates which might be relevant and useful two or three weeks ago might be entirely useless and irrelevant two or three weeks after. I would remind every reasonable man in this House that the Liberal platform of 1919 was laid down a few years before the general election, and those were years of crowding events, those were years when the financial situation of the country was becoming worse at a faster ratio even than we had feared. Consequently there is every reason to believe that the people took a sensible view of the issue's that were addressed to them in that long campaign which preceded December 6th last, when it is to be remembered the Liberal platform was two or three years old, which is a long time as events move these days. But to say, as did the hon. member for Vancouver South, that the people were deceived by the Liberal platform, when the right hon. leader of the Opposition himself avowed that he was going to have a long campaign for the express purpose of permitting a propaganda of education of the electorate, is a trifling with the plain facts of the case and with the intelligence of the people. In

that long campaign it so happened that the three parties presented the issues to the people fully and fairly, and the verdict shows that the people did not expect any sudden change in the tariff at this critical juncture. Therefore I believe the tariff as a whole is eminently satisfactory to the country, even though perforce private interests here and there fed the pinch of taxation that perhaps they think cannot be justified as entirely equitable.
It is common ground that we have a very hard country to govern. We look to Canada's north, and we have the plains of the eternal winter. Our Lady of the Snows will cast her smiles in vain in that direction if she expects to find her true destiny or her true affinity there. We look to the West, and almost in the extreme portion of it we find the barrier of the Rocky mountains-beauteous as God ever made; so beauteous that the tourist goes in there and gladly pays liberally for his enjoyment of them, incidentally affording us a small fraction of our revenue, something for which we are truly thankful. But those mountain ranges, unfortunately, are a barrier to traffic, and when we go to the Pacific coast and find the glittering waters of the Pacific ocean leaning against those mountain ranges we realize that the Pacific ocean herself is a jealous mistress, because she says to the inland Canadian: You may not bring your steaming trains westward to load freight on the ships that float upon my bosom. You may not send your steaming engines eastward, hauling trains with freight from those ships-this you cannot do until you have passed my outer guards, which are comprised in the sharp grades in those very mountains. Mr. Speaker, those grades are austere; they are hostile to traffic, as every man knows who tries to bring about complete interprovincial trade between East and the extreme West.
Will my hon. friend permit me a question? Is he aware that the grades on the Canadian National from Edmonton to the Coast are better than from Edmonton to Winnipeg?

I have not followed all the things that have been said in favour of this budget, but I have tried to follow everything that has been said against it, on its merits. As one hon. gentleman put it, the Minister of Finance has access to avenues of information that are not open to the ordinary member, and for myself I am willing again to trust the old financial pilot who brought us through those former fifteen budgets so successfully. Reasoning from analogy, I would expect the best possible results from this his sixteenth budget. I have heard very little in this debate in criticism of the budget on its merits. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), who I am sorry is not in his seat to-night, in what seemed to me a rather cheap sneer at the expense of Germany, beaten and

stricken as she is, said that to him this budget appeared as free trade with Germany and a 21 per cent reduction in favour of the United Kingdom. That statement was made for only one purpose, and a very demagogic purpose, a purpose, I submit, unworthy of any man who so recently occupied a seat as minister of the Crown in this country. I listened to the thoughtful address of the Progressive member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston), who made some criticism of the sales tax. I confess that several of his observations have impressed me. There is an important industry in my own town and those identified with it have written to me along the line that they consider that the sales tax on certain of their finished products is unfair. Now I think it was the duty of the leader of the Opposition to have discovered, if he could, what, on its merits, was wrong with this tariff. Perhaps I should not anticipate him, I have no doubt he will speak yet; but I will say this: There is nothing in the amendment itself which mentions anything whatsoever as wrong with the merits of this budget. The leader of the Opposition and those surrounding him are supposed to be the critics in this chamber. In addition to his regular indemnity the leader of the Opposition gets a substantial, and some would think a handsome, allowance for the purpose of being a sort of attorney to watch all the legislation that is brought down by the government. We all know the weakness to which the attorney
The Budget-Mr. Putman

for the defence is prone whose only resource, during the progress of the trial, is to abuse the attorney for the plaintiff; and it does seem to me very much as though the attorney for the defence, in the person of the leader of the Opposition, by setting up in the amendment this empty cry about lowering the standards of public life-by hurling that general accusation at those who have propounded this tariff-has resorted to the old device of merely abusing the attorney for the plaintiff.
Now is there anything so terrible about the violation of this platform for 1919 even to the extent which hon. gentlemen opposite have suggested? As I have pointed out, that platform was laid down in other times and under conditions not nearly so bad as they are revealed today. Why, Mr. Speaker, it is not unknown that the full intent and purpose of a promise may sometimes be very honourably modified, or the execution of the promise may sometimes be very honourably deferred, or sometimes the promise may very honourably be dropped out of sight and out of recollection altogether. Do you remember the last general election in England-and I suppose we are British enough to admit that the leaders of the political thought over there are men of honour-do you remember that that great leader of thought, Lloyd George, and his great associate in the Union government, Mr. Bonar Law, and all who surrounded them in that campaign, promised categorically and in specific terms that it was part of their platform that the Kaiser would be pulled out of Germany altogether and given a trial before the courts of England? As a matter of illustration, and just to show how specific that promise was, let me read the actual words of Lloyd George at that time:
We have decided that the man who undoubtedly had the prime responsibility for the war, in the judgment, at any rate, of the allied countries, should be tried for the offence he committed in breaking Treaties which he was bound in honour to respect, to which he was a party, and by that means bringing such horrors upon the world. The allied countries have decided quite unanimously that the tribunal shall be an Inter-Allied one, and that it shall sit in London for the trial of the person supremely responsible for this war.
I suppose that if the little group to your left, Mr. Speaker, were over in England to-night, and elected to the great legislative body there, they would have some amendment denouncing the honour of the public men of England for not having tried the Kaiser before this. But, Mr. Speaker, is

there any complaint on the part of the best public spirit and the best public opinion in England because that promise was dropped? I have never heard of any; it simply faded away in the light of second thought and of subsequent events. It is a promise which can never be kept. The Kaiser is growing old; it becomes more and more inhumane to think of carrying out that promise now. But the citadel of protection is still arrogant, is still impudent; and when we get out of the financial stress of this war, as we hope to some day; when we get through these dark hours of the railway deficits, as we are still hoping to do; there will come a time when all the promises of the 1919 Liberal platform can be revived; and if the hon. gentleman to whom I allude is right that the verdict of a few months ago was a verdict against high protection, a verdict in favour of the 1919 Liberal platform, it will not be a very courageous course one will have to take to try to implement all those promises.
Now referring once more to promises: Hon. gentlemen opposite have called themselves, within recent times, by several different names; and I heard the genial member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) the other night stand up and say that he declined to be called a Tory any longer. Now I have not had much experience in the art, the delight and the exhiliaration of playing cards, but I do believe that among the devotees of the games of the card table- especially among some of the more standard games-it is a rule that a good loser should stop while he is still losing. The man who quits while he is still losing is supposed to be a good sport, and on that principal I congratulate the hon. member for Fort William upon having the proclivities of a real good sport. But whatever the name-and perhaps it is none of my business-by which that group should be called, there is this about it that in years gone by they did seriously set themselves up as having the major part of the political wisdom of this country, and they persisted in that claim until the great Laurier came on the horizon in 1896 and gave Canada her fifteen golden years. Then that same group-whatever their name then or now-persisted very seriously in the claim that they had a monopoly of the loyalty and of the imperialistic spirit in this country; I am sorry to say they persisted in that claim right down until the time of the war when the Liberal blood was mixed in equal volume with the Tory blood which flowed into those horrible

We are not ashamed of that.

Certainly not, and
neither are we of the word "Tory". I can remember some years ago when I was a boy at school we always recognized that, in a time of dispute, the boy who got on top of the fence and proceeded to call names, did so because he lacked the necessary material to get down and put up a real argument. As long as hon. members opposite think criticism consists in throwing this word across the floor of the House, we in this corner may feel comparatively safe. But if the time should come, in the dim and distant future, when it is necessary for us to get up and apply epithets across the floor for lack of criticism, then they may well consider that they have reached a height of statesmanship that puts them above criticism. The previous speaker also in his closing remarks addressed himself to the Progressive party, and he called attention to the fact that he owed his election to hundreds, I think he said, of Progressives who supported him, for the very simple reason

that the Liberal platform and the Progressive platform were so nearly identical. I believe that is a fairly correct statement. So far as I was able to observe in the last campaign, the statement was made repeatedly that there was practically no difference between the two platforms, and that the Liberal party, if entrusted with the Government of the country, would prove equally the friend of the farmer and the labouring man as the Progressive party. I am sorry to say, however, that speeches so far contributed by members of the Progressive party show that in the present budget, they are not able to see the close resemblance.
Many complimentary things have been said in connection with the presentation of this budget by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I am sure they are well deserved; and it certainly is a distinction to be able to present in this House one's sixteenth budget. Possibly, however, this budget has presented greater difficulties than any of the preceding fifteen, so that, in attempting criticism of it, I, and I believe other hon. members as well, realize the difficulties confronting the Minister of Finance in the production of this budget and in our criticism we shall endeavour to be fair and courteous. I once heard a remarkable compliment paid the Minister of Finance by an old admirer of his, a gentleman who has been a life-long supporter of his party and who is an intense admirer of the minister personally. In discussing old times, this gentleman, who is well past the allotted span of life, said: "I consider that the present Minister of Finance is one of the most capable men in Canada."
Hear, hear.

Hon. members opposite say " hear, hear ", but let me tell the House the rest of it, please. He said: " Actually in 1896 his party was elected on a free-trade platform, and he was able after that to maintain and even increase the duties in some respects and get away with it." For that reason he considered him a great man of great ability. The same speaker said to me:	"On platform after platform at that time I preached the free-trade doctrine and, though I never believed a word of it myself, it was a great thing as a vote catcher." Now in my opinion, the minister to-day has a more difficult task than he had in 1896 to clear himself entirely in this regard.
I must, in passing, refer to a speech made this afternoon, and as it is in cornmon with a number of similar expressions made in this House, I think it is worthy of reference. We in this corner of the House have been told that our criticism is not constructive, and that we should offer an amendment of real constructive value. Well, we are not in authority, but I venture to say on behalf of my esteemed leader and of my associates that if the Government will say they are in need of, and will accept our advice we will tender it with the very best intentions. While possibly we may not feel free to offer advice on every occasion, I would remind my hon. friends opposite that we in this corner have, even this afternoon and on other occasions offered constructive criticism of the Government's proposals. Especially was that true in connection with the militia and naval estimates. But what was the result? One of the most influential members of the House, my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) in referring to our criticism and the plans we suggested in relation to those estimates said, "May I be permitted to add that the criticism and suggestions of the official Opposition only strengthens my purpose in asking for a reduction in the vote." Surely, Sir, in the face of such discouragement we have the interests of this country too much at heart to prejudice them by offering suggestions to such unsympathetic ears.
In the last election if there was one thing more than another the Liberal party claimed was nearest to their heart it was the welfare of the great masses, the common people. In looking up the debate on the budget last year I find that in a speech occupying about two hours and a half the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie
[Mr. Stansell. I
King) stated in effect that while the Conservative party might be thinking of the big interests and the specially privileged classes who were benefited by a protective tariff, he and his party were thinking of the welfare of the common people. I have not his speech at hand, but it may be found in Hansard of last year, commencing at page 3607.
Well, let us see how this budget bears out his professions. The effect of a protective tariff upon the public was never better described than in the words of one who at least was noted for his sympathy with the common people and his ability as a statesman; I refer to Abraham Lincoln. He said: When we purchase goods in a foreign country we get the goods and the foreigner gets the money; when we purchase goods made at home we get both the goods and the money. No one has yet put the matter in a more practical form; no one yet has ever offered any conclusive argument against the truth of his view. But, Sir, it is claimed that under a protective tariff abuses will grow up. This may be so, but we also know that abuses creep into many of the good things of this life. I am perfectly frank in saying that I believe in a protective policy, and I also believe that that policy is best adapted to the needs of this country to-day, although sufficient care should be exercised in tariff revision from time to time to see that it is closely adjusted to the needs of the day, for in five or ten years' time conditions may alter and therefore necessitate a revision.
Some hon. members in the course of this debate have complained that where our revenue is raised by a tariff the full benefit does not accrue to the treasury, a considerable portion of the duties going into the pockets of the manufacturers or protectionists as they are termed. I am quite willing to grant that, but I think hon. members will also agree with me that it is in the best interest of this country to as far as possible purchase commodities that are produced at home. I am sure those who are familiar with farming will not dispute me when I say-and this applies especially to mixed farming with which I am familiar-that the successful farmer does not purchase what he is able to produce on his own farm; but -as far as may be practical produces his own requirements. The contrary policy leads to one result- bankruptcy. Of course, we cannot produce everything we require, but the country as a whole might be compared to a great big

The Budget-Mr. Stansell
farm, and surely what is good for the unit is good for the whole. We should have a policy that encourages as far as possible the production of goods at home, and in so far as that is practical and compatible with good judgment we should support such a policy.
In this connection it is obvious that we should encourage the maximum production of goods at home to meet the wants of our people, and this can only be accomplished in a practical way by a customs tariff. I am not a particular friend of any manufacturing industry, but surely it is a good policy to do something in a national way to encourage the investment of capital for the development of our own country, because then we have the opportunity to tax that capital to meet our national expenses; but it is absolutely impossible to obtain revenue in this way from foreign corporations who export their goods to this country. In this way the operation of the tariff accomplishes both purposes: it encourages the investment of capital in domestic enterprises, and it also increases our national revenue.
But the budget is wrong in this respect that while it reduces the tariff, thereby of course making a bid for the support of the working men and the farmers, at the same time it increases the sales tax by 50 per cent, which tax applies to practically everything the people require. The great masses of the consumers are the working men and the farmers-the common people, and they are compelled to contribute more than their share to the revenue of the country, although they are less able to do that than those classes who by reason of their smaller consumption of the necessaries of life are able to escape with a lighter share of the burden. Therefore this Government which professed to have so much at heart the interests of the masses have failed to live up to their professions, for undoubtedly working people with large families and small incomes are compelled by this increased sales tax to pay more for the necessaries of life, and in that respect in my judgment the budget is a serious mistake. Those who studied carefully the Liberal platform-the farmer, the labouring many or any other class of the electorate who hoped for relief from taxation from that source-will derive little comfort from a budget of this character. In replying to a question this afternoon the Minister of Finance said he expected that notwithstanding the reduction of the tariff he would get an increased revenue. Now, we

know that if there is an increased revenue it can only come by increased purchases in a foreign country. If we are to deal with the problems which face the farmer and the workingman by building up the big interests in foreign countries, increasing our purchases there and thus adding to the unemployment in our own country; if we are to do that and then offset the reductions in the tariff by the operation of a sales tax to secure the money from the pockets of our own people, I say it is a serious mistake and one not in keeping with the promises and platform of the Liberal party before they attained power.
How does the hon. member suggest that the farmer, especially the western farmer, could sell his products abroad without buying abroad?

How do you sell your wheat, may I ask? I have understood from the discussion arising out of the application for a wheat board that the market for wheat was largely in Great Britain. We have never had any trouble in getting a market for our wheat there. It is true we are shut out of the American market, but that is due to the action of our neighbours to the south and not to tariff barriers on our part. Now, I did anticipate the asking of this question: How do we get the revenue from the protected interests, if we must call them such?

Would the hon. gentleman permit me another question? He says that our market for wheat is in Great Britain. Now, if he could prevent Britain from exporting manufactured articles, would our market in Britain for our wheat continue ?
I would answer that question if I had ever suggested anything of the kind, but I have not, and so far as I know, the suggestion has not been made by anybody in this part of the House.
Did the hon. member not suggest a few moments ago that it would be to the advantage of this country to buy cur goods in Canada and not abroad?

So far as practicable, yes. Does the hon. member not believe that that is a good policy? I was saying that the question I thought that might be asked was this: How will we obtain the necessary money, if we do not obtain it through the increased sales tax? By the very plan I spoke of a while ago,-a plan that was first put into operation by this party iwhen
The Budget-Mr. Millar

m power, and one that I believe to be the best system yet devised; a system that I hope will be continued by whatever party is in power-that of income taxation. By that method alone can we compel the man who gets more than his share of this world's goods to contribute a proper share to the . revenues of the country. My policy, Mr. Speaker, would be one that would encourage the investment of capital in this country and the taxation of wealth where it is found rather than one that would encourage the building up of industries in a foreign country where we have no power to impose taxation. Under the latter condition we must obtain our revenue largely from the pockets of the poor man, of the labouring man and the farmer. In this respect the present budget fails. I offer that criticism, and I believe it can safely be called constructive criticism.
The question may be asked, why has the sales tax been increased? I think I can safely say that in a time like this, when revenue is so necessary, there is sure to be some objection to almost any form of taxation. But there is one large section of our people who have no means of audibly speaking for themselves, no method by which they can present their case in this House. I refer to the great mass of the consumers. This sales tax, no matter on what it is applied, is handed on from one to another until it reaches that class of the people, and for the reason that they are less able to offer objection, it is the special form of taxation which is easy to enforce, and easy to collect. But it is pernicious in its form and effect and utterly fails to provide a solution of the pressing problem presented by our numbers of unemployed and because it does not fulfil the pre-election pledges of its party I propose to vote for the amendment.

Mr. -Speaker, before addressing myself to the budget, I would like to offer a word of congratulation to the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding). I feel a pride in realizing that we have a finance minister who is able at the age of seventy-three to perform such a difficult task with such signal success.
In discussing the budget, I think it is recognized by every one in this House and out of it, that vast sums of money are necessary in the administration of the country's affairs. We ran into heavy debt during *the war. I have one criticism to offer of my hon. friends to my right, and it is that during the war years more of the cost of the

war should have been raised. I have seen the statement-and I -believe it is correct- that only six per cent of the cost of the war was raised by Canada during the war years, while Great Britain and the United States raised upwards of thirty per cent- in fact, I am not sure it was not over forty per cent. Those were years when money was fairly plentiful in Canada. Those were years in which the farmer was receiving good prices for his products, in which contracts were being let for war supplies. As I say, money was plentiful, and I believe money could have been raised more easily then than it can now. I see no reason why thirty or forty per cent of the cost of the war could not have been raised by Canada during those years. I do not think many of our people were benefited by the easy *money they received. We fell into expensive personal habits; these habits still cling to our people, and that is one obstacle that stands in the way of our getting back to normal conditions. Once we acquire these expensive habits, both business and personal, we come to believe we cannot get along without them. If the late government had levied quite a stiff tax at that time and had taken in a considerable quantity of the ready money then available, they would have stabilized income and conferred benefit all round, and we would not now have the enormous national debt under which we are labouring.
I think we all realize that the time should soon come when our receipts should equal our outgo, when we should be paying our own way and bringing a stop to the increase of our national debt. I have, therefore, no abjection to make to the vast amount which is proposed to be raised by the Finance Minister. A budget should be so framed as to encourage 'basic industries. It may be otherwise in industrial Great Britain, but in Canada I am sure that the money that is lavished on the cities will not have the effect of making the agricultural interests or classes prosperous. But the reverse is true. If you make the agricultural interest, the mining and lumbering and fishing interests prosperous, you bring prosperity to the urban centres as well; it cannot be otherwise. During the years that have passed I think all will realize that the agricultural industry has been bled white. That is the condition now, whether we realize it or not. How has that been accomplished? Let me go back for a moment. I can remember the time many years ago when some industries believed that cut-throat competition was

The Budget-Mr. Millar
not in their interest, and wanting to get rid of it, they got together and held meetings and made agreements, which sometimes held and sometimes not, but there was the first attempt to form a monopoly. As the years went by, they succeeded better, and now the time has come when from the barber to the banker we have monopolies, small and large, in every industry. If you go to the barber he has his price list, and he must not charge less, though he may charge more. It is the same in other industries, even in the noble profession of medicine, and if I were picking out one profession as a noble one I would pick out the doctors, yet even they have their price list, below which they must not go, although they may charge more.
Is that done in the West?
It is certainly done in the West.
It is not done in Ontario. I belong to that profession.

As it is now, when we purchase goods we purchase from small monopolies. The agricultural interest has progressed in the same direction for the reason that a large part of our product must be sold on the world's market. We must compete against Russia, the Argentine, India and other wheat-growing countries of the world, and no act of this Parliament can raise the price of wheat more than perhaps a fraction of a cent. That being the case, when overhead charges are piled up on the agriculturists they must either go out of growing grain for export-in fact, they are forced to go out of grain growing so far as export is concerned. I believe that during the past ten or fifteen years if Russia had been as proficient as we are in our methods of agriculture, and had had the same efficient transportation system as we have in this country, Canada could not have exported one bushel of wheat; we could not have competed with her. It is only because of their crude methods that we are able to export wheat. However, that is another matter.
I have spoken of small monopolies, and while it seems to me that Parliament should have done something to check the small monopolies, it has really done something to encourage them. But our greatest monopoly is caused by the customs tariff. Before
coming to that, let me say that I make no objection whatever to the various industries of the country forming their unions. I believe it is well that Labour should have its unions. They have done much to advance the welfare of the labouring classes and to win for them greater consideration, but when they arbitrarily fix the remuneration they shall receive from the rest of society for the contribution they are making to society, I believe it is wrong. I believe it is wrong for other industries to have that privilege. I have been struck by this during the discussions on the Wheat Board. Some strong advocates of protection have been greatly alarmed lest the establishment of the Wheat Board should lead to co-operation between the various nations so that they would be able arbitrarily to fix the price of wheat. That is, they are very much alarmed lest the policy they themselves advocate should be carried to its logical conclusion. We know what would happen if that should ever come to pass. Those who were able to control foodstuffs would starve the rest of the world, and in a small way that is what is being done by small monopolies at the present time.
I had hoped that this new Government when formed would be able to match its ingenuity against the ingenuity of man. During past years various corporations and individuals have found a way of circumventing legislation and of extracting large profits from the consumer. They have found a way of getting around the law, and our Parliament has not kept pace. I had hoped that when the new budget came down we should have had some evidence that the present Government had the initiative and the ability to cope with those who have been thus evading the law and extracting profits from the consumer to which they have no right, and I am sure that undue profits (are being taken. A financial expert speaking to the Manufacturers' Association in Toronto a short time ago said, in effect: Quit breaking the Ten Commandments, and then you will have prosperity. I believe that when the various interests in Canada give a little more consideration to other interests, show a little more sympathy, and are willing to help not merely their own constituencies first but all parts of Canada that need help, we shall be taking a step towards prosperity. We have been following too much in the past the rule of give and take- give as little as possible, and take all you can get.

The Budget-Mr. Millar
I had hoped that the reduction in the customs tariff-it is not the whole remedy for the depression that is burdening Canada at the present time, but still it is one of the remedies-would have been much greater than it is. A reduction of 21 per cent is not sufficient to place agriculture on its feet. On an article where the duty is 30 or 35 per cent, a small cut of 21 per cent means very little. It is some relief certainly; it is a step in the right direction, and if it had been twice as large and was to be followed up next session by another similar cut, I would have had no complaint to make, because I think it was understood all through the country-I know it was in the constituency I represent-that it would not be wise to make drastic changes all at once, and that industry should be allowed to adjust itself to the changed condition.
Just one word more about the conditions in agriculture. I look upon the law of the survival of the fittest as quite sound. Under normal conditions, if an occasional man engaged in farming or any other business is a misfit, not the most capable, and is compelled to make an assignment and drop out and find some other occupation, it keeps that industry in a fairly healthy condition. I have no complaint with that, but it is quite a different matter when a whole class is being crushed, and I assure you that that is the condition at the present time with agriculture in most, I will not say all, parts of Canada. In some parts of Canada where mixed farming and fruit growing are carried on the markets are fairly satisfactory. Some parts of Canada may be said to be fairly prosperous but throughout the greater part of the Dominion agriculture is languishing. In the case of small monopolies the remedy, I believe, is largely in the hands of the people themselves; and so long, and so far, as the people can themselves, by co-operation, remedy the grievances under which they are suffering, they have no right to come to any government and ask for assistance, and as far as possible governments should not interfere. But there are times when it is necessary for governments to do so. In the case of such national monopolies as the Imperial Oil Company, for instance, what can the people of Canada do if they are not given some support and assistance by their legislators either in the Dominion or provincial House? Many people have asked during the last few years why it is that gasoline, to give a concrete example, should be retailing in Canada for 50 cents a gallon, when the retail' charge on the 
other side of the line is only 25 cents a gallon. True the American gallon is not quite as large as the Canadian gallon, but the difference is very trifling. We have a country very rich in oil, immensely rich, to be accurate; and yet during the month of March last, and I suppose the same con-' dition exists to-day, we were paying at the retail stations twice the price for gasoline that they were paying on the American side of the boundary. In the case of such monopolies as these, the aim of a budget should be, as far as possible, to so direct industry as to prevent such abuses.
I am now going to read extracts from the utterances of three of our public men on the tariff. Two of these statesmen have passed from this life; the other, I am very pleased to say, is still with us. The late Sir Richard Cartwright said in speaking of the tariff:
The moment you introduce the protective system you create a class whose interests are essentially different from those of the people at large and who become ready contributors to corruption funds sharing with their masters the plunder which they have been able to take from the people.
In 1893 the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
One of the evils of the National Policy has been here as everywhere else, to lower the morale of public life.
And again he said:
If you want to purify the political atmosphere not a cent must be levied except what is necessary to carry on the legitimate expenses of the government economically administered.
Now I think perhaps hon. members to the right will listen to the next extract quite attentively. Speaking before parliament ,on January 18, 1922, the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) said:
