Another objection to the customs tariff- the National Policy as we have known it- is that it leads to mergers. Here is an instance; it is an example, I suppose, that has been cited many times but there are some things that will bear repetition, "lest we forget". The Canada Cement Company, organized in 1909, swallowed up eleven concerns having a total capitalization of $17,750,000. It was itself organized with a capitalization of $38,000,000. In July, 1909, the city of Winnipeg purchased 25 thousand barrels of cement at $1.77. Five months later, after the merger had -taken place, the best offer they could get from three tenders from different agents of the Canada Cement Company was $2.24, an increase of 47 cents per barrel. In 1917 the total domestic production of cement in Canada was $7,007,000 and the importation was $26,000. This means that, at the retail rate of $2.50 per cwt. as a unit there were 3,000,000 units locally produced and about 10,000 units imported, so that the -sum of $300,000 was paid as a bonus to the Canada Cement Company. Not only this but only a thousand dollars went into the public treasury as duty on $26,000 worth of cement. An examination of the facts in regard to other articles would lead to a similar conclusion.
Now let -me say a word in regard to the tariff of 1906-1907. Within a week after they were afforded protection, the -three
companies who manufactured print cloth in Canada advanced their prices, and while the Customs Act was still awaiting the Royal Assent a statement appeared in the Globe of Toronto which showed the conditions prevailing at the time when the increase was made. The article in question stated:
With regard to the ability of the mills to keep u-p to the demand, wholesalers declare that in the case of Canadian prints and domestic cottons, the situation is growing worse instead of improving, and that with prices steadily advancing it is becoming harder than ever to get deliveries.
In 1905 when the duties on white lead were increased from 5 to 30 and 35 per cent, the manufacturers were so eager to take toll from the Canadian people that telegrams were sent to their commercial travellers to add these percentages immediately to their price lists.
Now I would like to say a word in regard to the sales tax. I was very sorry indeed to see the sales tax increased because it certainly hits the poor man. Taxes that are imposed should be in proportion to -people's ability to pay. In the eleven months up to end of April, 1921, during which it was in operation, the sales tax brought in $40,898,383. As a producer of revenue it failed most when money was most needed. In October 1920, when business was good and retail prices were still high, the collections were $5,020,476, but in April they fell to $2,873,219, and were -still falling when the tax was increased. In the six months that the luxury taxes were in operation they brought in $2,000,000 more than the sales tax realized in the whole eleven months. I do not know just why the luxury tax was taken off. There may have been good reasons, but I think it would have been much better policy to tax luxuries than to tax those things that are necessary for the poor people, which all poor people must have, if they are going to live. The sales tax is not equitable, for no other reason than that the poor man, who must spend practically all he earns, pays the tax out of what should go for necessaries, whereas the rich man pays it out of surplus. The rich man who spends several months out of Canada escapes this tax, whereas the poor man, who cannot have any holiday, must pay it all the time.

Another comment I have to make on the national policy is that it confuses two functions of government that should he entirely separate and distinct. Without making any personal application either to the present Finance Minister or any past Finance Minister, I wish to say that when we find a man in Canada who is so highly trained along the lines of finance and most capable to handle the financial affairs of our country, we will seldom find that that same man is most highly trained along the line necessary to develop and foster industry, and yet we have combined the two. The same individual is expected to perform the two functions. Then, again, at present it is impossible for the people of Canada to know how much it costs them to foster those industries. Is that sound business? Would you find any business man following such a policy in his own business? He wants to know what part of his business is paying, and what part is not paying? In this case we cannot tell. We can only make a guess. The question arises, if this protection is swept away, what are the manufacturers to do? I believe there are a few that should be swept away, but not very many. We want the manufacturers, as far as we can have them, but the people of Canada should know what it

The Budget-Mr. Millar
is costing them to have those manufacturers. If it cost the country $10,000,000 to have a certain article manufactured in Canada and it is worth only $3,000,000 to Canada-if Canada is reaping only $3,000,000 because it is here-it is about time that such a manufacture should cease.
The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Stansell) said that he thought it was a good thing for a farmer to grow all he could and not to have to buy. When a farmer can buy from his neighbour for $5 an article that it costs him $10 to produce, it is a far wiser thing for him to buy. His neighbour, on the other hand, may want to buy from him an article that the first farmer referred to can produce much more cheaply than the other. I think we will agree that what has made the United States prosperous has been the free interchange of commodities or free trade amongst the different states.

I am well aware that, owing to the nature of some soils, one farmer can produce what another cannot. I said that, so far as was practicable, it was good policy for a farmer to produce as much as he could on his own farm.

Following that argument, let me state that other nations, because of their different climates and conditions, can produce some articles very much more cheaply than we can. A few days ago I noticed in the paper where a cutlery firm in the city of Kingston stated that Germany could place in Canada for 69 cents a dozen knives that it cost this firm $4 to produce. I would like- very much to know just what it is costing Canada to keep that industry going. I am inclined to think where there is such a difference as that, if the people of Canada knew what it was costing them to keep that industry going, they would cease paying, ' and that industry would have to go out of business. I agree with my hon. friend to my right that, so far as possible, we should give some consideration to the different conditions, and to cheaper labour in the Old Country market. But I would far rather see Canada resort to the principle, objectionable as it may be, of paying bonuses, so that the people of Canada might know exactly what they were paying, than have the present system of protection.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up the time of the House to any great extent; but I must first offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) upon being able to bring down his sixteenth budget. I have nothing further upon which I can congratulate him than on being in that position.
Before dealing with the budget, I wish to make a few remarks in regard to what has been said by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar). I know he does not want in any way whatever to create any false impression in this House. He first said that six per cent of the war expenditure was paid out of the revenue of this country. The late government, in the last year of its existence, paid $553,000,000 of the war expenditure, or a little over 20 per cent, or roughly, about 22 per cent. There is quite a difference between that and six per cent. The hon. member also referred to the Canada Cement Company. This was a merger which was effected under the regime of the Liberal government in 1909, and the duty was reduced by the Conservative government in 1912. He also said that the income tax was adopted at the suggestion, or on the advice, of the United Farmers or the Council of Agriculture, which did not happen to be in existence at that time, but for argument's sake, we will say that it was. The party, however, to which he refers, if they were able to gain anything at that time from the Conservative government, have not so far been able to gain very much from the present administration.
The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) this afternoon dwelt at some length on the 21 per cent reduction in the tariff on agricultural implements. He compared the cost of an agricultural implement costing $100, plus duty under the old budget of 121 per cent and sales tax of $4.50, making a total cost of $117, with the cost of that same implement under the present budget, which reduces the duty to 10 per cent and increases the sales tax to $6.60, making a total cost of $116.60, or a saving of 40 cents. But we might reduce that saving by the four cents which the purchaser will have to pay on his cheque, leaving him a net advantage of 36 cents.
The increase in the British preference is to my mind a step in the right direction as it will encourage trade with the Old

Country. In this connection I noticed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was not very successful in his trip to Washington to secure closer trade relations with the United States. Since that occasion the Fordney bill has been before Congress, and as hon. members are aware it practically prohibits the sale of our products to the United States. For instance, American wheat can come in here free of duty, while we have to pay 35 cents a bushel on our wheat entering the United States. On American eggs we impose a duty of three cents a dozen, as against a duty of eight cents a dozen on our eggs entering the States. Various other commodities might be instanced on which there is a similar disparity in the respective duties. If any sane person would continue to do business with any one who treated him in that way I should be inclined to question his sanity.
We have been advised through the press of the various measures of economy which this Government from time to time was supposed to be introducing. But I believe that the economy effected will not in the long run save the country any money, on the contrary it will prove to be false economy. For instance, according to the estimates we find there is an increase of $51,256.18 for civil government. At the same time we know that there have been about five hundred dismissals from various branches of the civil service. That is an instance of the kind of economy the Government is practising.
And along with these dismissals comes a reduction in the bonus to civil servants. To my mind the bonus should have been left as it was or if altered at all it should have been in an upward direction. Civil servants without dependents are practically stripped of the bonus. It seems to me appropriate to remind the Government that a little while ago the sessional indemnity was increased from $2,500 to $4,000, and I suppose that it will foe the policy of the Government to see that all private members and Cabinet ministers without dependents shall revert to the old indemnity. I think that is only fair if the Government are to be consistent in the policy they have adopted towards the civil service.
I am sorry that neither of the members for the city of Ottawa is in his seat tonight. I do not want to take an unfair advantage of them, but I fully expected that they would have expressed their views on the bonus long before this. The Citizen of November 8th, 1921, reports the senior

Mr. Speaker, in rising to add my quota to this [DOT]debate on the budget, I would like in the first place to pass some more bouquets to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I have been pleased in the past to read a great many of his 'budget addresses, and, Sir, I am certain of one thing: that he is possessed of the art of making figures pleasant. The hon. minister has delivered *more budget speeches than any other man in the British dominions-two more, even, than the Right Hon. William Ewart Gladstone.
Before I start to talk about the budget I would like to say to the hon. gentlemen on my right, as well as those on the other side, that I object to their referring to hon. members in this part of the House as westerners. We are not westerners; there were more Progressive members elected in

The Budget-Mr. J. W. King
the old banner province of Ontario than in any other province. If the province of New Brunswick had elected twenty-three more, they would have elected as many as Ontario did.
Now, in referring to the budget, I shall not discuss it item by item. I am a new parliamentarian, Ibut I understand that the items will be taken up later. In a broad sense, Sir, I want to say that in my view the fiscal policy of Canada up to the present time has been a wrong policy. Canada's present population is 8,746,872 souls. Canada's land area, exclusive of the Northwest Territories, and1 the Yukon, and exclusive also of swamp lands which at the present time are nonproductive, but which may at some future time become productive, comprises 1,401,100,000 acres. Of these, 31 per cent, or 440,000,000 acres are fit for cultivation; only 101,000,000 acres are occupied and only 60,000,000 acres, or less than 16 per cent, are under cultivation. Now, Canada is over 200 years of age, and why is this the case? It is because, Sir, her fiscal policy has been such that her people have been congregating in the cities. The result of the fiscal policy which has been carried out in Canada, since Confederation at all events, has been a tendency on the part of the people to drift into the cities. We hope that the present Government, if they are in power, will continue in the direction they have faced. They have made a very short step in the right direction, and we hope they will continue in it, so that ultimately they may adopt a different fiscal policy.
I may say to my friends on my right that I have no objection to fostering infant industries to a certain extent, though I do object to supporting them too long. I heard Sir John A. Macdonald in the early eighties-and I heard him personally in my own county; I am not giving any hearsay evidence-declare before an audience made up largely of farmers: "You farmers have hewn out homes for yourselves in the bush in the county of Huron; you are in comparatively easy circumstances, and I wish to lay a burden on your backs for the purpose of helping infant industries1, for the purpose of starting high smokestacks all over the Dominion of Canada." But tie said also that he would not allow that burden to remain upon the people longer than a period of fifteen or twenty years. Now, *Sir John A. Macdonald died in 1891, and1 I believe if he had lived the party to my right would be heading in a different direction fiscally. I do not believe that he in-

tended for one moment to continue that tariff policy indefinitely. Moreover, he said on that same occasion that at such time as the home manufacturer got such a grip on his infant industry that he began to export, at that moment the tariff would be cut.
Now, without going into minutise, I want to say that if there is any chance of our having reciprocity with the United States we should1 try to get it. There is no doubt that all wealth in this country has to emanate from four sources-from agriculture, from the mine, from the forest and from the sea. If you make the agriculturists in this country prosperous, you will make everybody prosperous. The Mas-sey-Harris Company a year ago, when they found that the purchasing power of the farmer was at an end, stopped production, and that is the idea that is carried out by all the manufacturers. I will mention no names, but I heard one hon. member to my right say that, having some land, he thought he would engage in the dairying industry; accordingly he bought 30 or 40 cows, but when he found they did not pay, he stopped production. Now, we farmers are made of sterner stuff; we do not stop production. I am reminded of a story I once read of Napoleon Bonaparte at the battle of Waterloo, when his soldiers captured a small British drummer boy. The boy was brought before the great general, who said to him: "Play the march". The boy played the march, whereupon the general said: "Very good; now play the charge." So the boy played the charge, and the general said: "You have done very well, my boy; now play the retreat." The boy replied: "Monsieur, I never learned to play the retreat; the British soldiers never retreat." Now, the Canadian farmer never retreats; he is made of sterner stuff. Even if he does not make ends meet; even if he has no profits at the end of the year, he still continues.
With regard to the possibilities of arranging a reciprocity treaty with the United States, I would say in the first place that nearly all the newspapers of the United States are thoroughly opposed to the present tariff proposals which are being discussed by the United States Senate. More than that, the Republican papers which represent the high protectionists of the United States are saying to the people: We cannot go to the country at the next presidential election on these grounds. If we do, President Harding is

The Budget-Mr. J. W. King
defeated. I do not think for one moment that it will be longer than four or five years before there will be a completely different fiscal policy in the United States. I wish to read a few extracts from American journals in that regard. The New York Journal of Commerce calls the Senate high tariff, "a bill to raise living costs and hamper trade."
The New York Tribune warns the Republican party that this is no time to go tariff mad, and that if President Harding stands for reelection it will be unfair to hamper him with this tariff as President Taft was hampered in 1912 by the Payne-Aldrich Act.
The St. Louis Globe-Democrat says that the new tariff applies protection without regard to new conditions of world trade and the change of the United States from a debtor to a creditor nation.
The Boston Transcript declares that the manufacturers are nearly paralyzed by war expenses and lack of markets, and are to some extent prepared to regard strikes as a blessing.
The New York Herald sees the United States shut out of foreign markets except in raw materials, notably cotton and copper.
The New York Post regards the tariff as making a present to Europe of eleven billion dollars owed to the United States. Europe cannot pay in gold and her goods will be excluded.
The United States has to import in order to get her debts paid, for she is no longer a debtor nation, hut a creditor nation. The New York World and the New York Times are virtually in opposition to the measure. Even the farm papers are not all favourable. I quote:
The Southland Farmer of Houston, Texas, regards the Bill as a betrayal of agriculture, bring the West and South under still greater bondage to the industrial sections of the East and North.
The New York American Agriculturalist favours the duties on certain farm products but wants fertilizing salts and other things needed on the farm to come in duty free so as to cheapen production.
Even the farmer bloc are not all in agreement on this measure, and they will find out that their prices are set at Liverpool, where they have to compete with our wheat.
Commenting on the changes made by the Fielding tariff the New York Commercial says:
But what is to be our attitude toward "protection" of those commodities which we normally import from Canada? Nothing has been gained by excluding Canadian wheat, for instance, from our markets only to force it to Liverpool, there to compete with ours just as effectively as it would in Chicago. The same or closely similar situations exist with regard to a good many other Canadian products. Can we gain our own consent to take a leaf from Canada's note book and adopt a more reasonable policy in such matters?
I could go on reading extracts to show the trend of opinion in the United States at the present time, but 1 shall not further weary the House. Any one who watches the trend of events to-day in the United States knows that it is towards freer trade relations with the whole world, and with Canada in particular. We and the United States are the same kith and kin. We are of the same blood. We speak practically the same language, and therefore on all these grounds there should be friendly relations between the two countries. I believe the present is a very opportune time to establish better relations, and I think we can depend upon the present Minister of Finance more than any other man in Canada to get along with the United States.
One gentleman on my right came along a moment ago and asked how long I was going to speak. I said, " Ten or fifteen minutes," so he tapped me on the back and said, " That is right." Mr. Speaker, I shall not make a motion, but I believe during this debate the speakers should confine themselves to speeches of fifteen or at the most twenty minutes. I do not believe that anything that is said in this debate will change one vote, for every man has al-already made up his mind. I shall not take up the time of the House further.
